\">\u003cfigcaption>Figure · page 4\u003c/figcaption>\u003c/figure>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">3. Correct cuff size and  placement\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Use an appropriate cuff\u003cbr>based on mid-arm\u003cbr>circumference. The\u003cbr>inflatable bladder should\u003cbr>cover most of the upper\u003cbr>arm circumference and\u003cbr>length. A cuff that is too\u003cbr>small gives falsely high\u003cbr>BP; a cuff that is too\u003cbr>large may give falsely\u003cbr>low BP.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Place the cuff on the\u003cbr>bare upper arm, about\u003cbr>2–3 cm above the\u003cbr>antecubital fossa, with\u003cbr>the artery marker over\u003cbr>the brachial artery. The\u003cbr>arm should be relaxed\u003cbr>and supported at heart\u003cbr>level.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">4. How many readings  to take in clinic\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Do not diagnose\u003cbr>hypertension from one\u003cbr>casual reading unless the\u003cbr>patient has hypertensive\u003cbr>emergency with acute\u003cbr>target-organ damage.\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 5\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">For routine clinic diagnosis:\u003c/p>\u003cdiv class=\"table-scroll\">\u003ctable class=\"clinical-table\">\u003ctr>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Step\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>What to do\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>First visit\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Measure BP in both arms\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>If different\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Use the arm with the higher reading for future measurements\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>During each visit\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Take at least 2 readings, 1 minute apart\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>If readings differ\u003cbr>significantly\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Take a third reading\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Diagnosis\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Use the average of repeated readings over at least 2 separate\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>visits\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003c/table>\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Diagnosis\u003cbr>Use the average of repeated readings over at least 2 separate\u003cbr>visits\u003cbr>AHA/ACC guidance emphasizes accurate measurement and repeated readings; clinical practice\u003cbr>guidelines recommend repeating BP measurements on two or more occasions before diagnosing\u003cbr>hypertension.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">5. First visit: measure both arms\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">At the first assessment, BP should be measured in both arms. If one arm is consistently higher,\u003cbr>document it and use that arm for future readings.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">A persistent inter-arm difference may suggest:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  peripheral arterial disease,    •  subclavian stenosis,    •  aortic disease,  •   vascular obstruction.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">6. Standing BP: when to check postural BP\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Measure lying/sitting and standing BP in patients at risk of orthostatic hypotension, especially:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•\u003cbr>elderly patients,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>diabetes,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>autonomic neuropathy,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Parkinsonism,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>recurrent dizziness/falls,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>dehydration,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>patients on diuretics, alpha-blockers, nitrates, or multiple antihypertensives.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">How to do it:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">1. Measure BP after lying or sitting for 5 minutes.\u003cbr>2. Ask patient to stand.\u003cbr>3. Measure BP at 1 minute and 3 minutes after standing.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Orthostatic hypotension is suggested by:\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 6\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  fall in SBP ≥20 mmHg, or    •  fall in DBP ≥10 mmHg, within 3 minutes of standing.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">7. Home BP monitoring\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Home BP is useful to confirm diagnosis, detect white-coat hypertension, detect masked\u003cbr>hypertension, and improve follow-up.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Correct home BP method:\u003c/p>\u003cdiv class=\"table-scroll\">\u003ctable class=\"clinical-table\">\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Timing\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>What patient does\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Morning\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Measure before breakfast and before BP medicines\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Evening\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Measure before supper/bed\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Each sitting\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Take 2 readings, 1 minute apart\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Duration\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Do this for 3–7 days\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Interpretation\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Average the readings, excluding day 1 if possible\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003c/table>\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Interpretation\u003cbr>Average the readings, excluding day 1 if possible\u003cbr>The American Heart Association advises being still, resting for at least 5 minutes before\u003cbr>measuring, avoiding talking, using a cuff on bare skin, and taking measurements correctly at\u003cbr>home.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">8. Ambulatory BP monitoring\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Ambulatory BP monitoring is the best method when available. It is useful for:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•\u003cbr>suspected white-coat hypertension,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>suspected masked hypertension,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>resistant hypertension,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>episodic hypertension,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>hypotensive symptoms on treatment,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>pregnancy hypertension assessment where available.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">It records BP over 24 hours and gives daytime, nighttime, and average BP.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Baseline investigations should include FBP, serum creatinine/eGFR, urea, sodium, potassium,\u003cbr>fasting/random glucose or HbA1c, lipid profile, urinalysis or urine ACR, ECG, and fundoscopy\u003cbr>where available. Do echocardiography if there is suspected hypertensive heart disease, heart\u003cbr>failure, murmur, or LVH. In young patients, resistant hypertension, hypokalemia, renal bruit,\u003cbr>abrupt onset, or severe hypertension, evaluate for secondary hypertension.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Management — Tanzania Practical Regime First\u003c/h4>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 7\u003c/div>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">1. Lifestyle modification for all patients\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">All hypertensive patients need lifestyle treatment, whether or not drugs are started. Advise salt\u003cbr>reduction, weight reduction, regular aerobic exercise, stopping smoking, limiting alcohol,\u003cbr>DASH-style diet with fruits/vegetables, avoiding NSAIDs where possible, and improving\u003cbr>adherence.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">WHO and AHA both emphasize lifestyle therapy as a core intervention, including sodium\u003cbr>restriction, physical activity, weight control, and alcohol reduction. The 2025 AHA/ACC update\u003cbr>also emphasizes home BP monitoring and cardiovascular risk-based treatment.\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 8\u003c/div>\u003cfigure class=\"note-figure\">\u003cimg loading=\"lazy\" alt=\"Illustration associated with page 8\" src=\"data:image/webp;base64,
